overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of Husserl's account of the lifeworld and of others. You'll be asked about the lifeworld, Galileo's mathematization of nature, the garb of ideas, the surreptitious substitution, and empathy and pairing.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are features of the lifeworld, on Husserl's account? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: It is pregiven, always already there before inquiry
options.text: It is pregiven, always already there before inquiry
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! We don't construct the lifeworld. We find ourselves in it.

options.html: It is prescientific, preceding and grounding theory
options.text: It is prescientific, preceding and grounding theory
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Every scientific concept starts from something given in the lifeworld.

options.html: It is shared, a common world experienced with others
options.text: It is shared, a common world experienced with others
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The lifeworld isn't a private world of sensations. It's experienced together with others.

options.html: It is the idealized world described by mathematical physics
options.text: It is the idealized world described by mathematical physics
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's the garb of ideas laid over the lifeworld, not the lifeworld itself.

options.html: It is the world of a person's private sensations only
options.text: It is the world of a person's private sensations only
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The lifeworld is shared, not private.

forms.stemHtml: How did Galileo's mathematization treat sensory qualities such as color and warmth?

options.html: As the true properties of bodies, directly measurable by instruments
options.text: As the true properties of bodies, directly measurable by instruments
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Sensory qualities can't be measured directly the way shapes can. Galileo treated them as indirectly mathematizable, through changes in shape and motion.

options.html: As indirectly mathematizable through changes in shape and motion
options.text: As indirectly mathematizable through changes in shape and motion
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The sensory plena couldn't be measured directly, so Galileo treated each change in quality as corresponding to a measurable change in shape and motion.

options.html: As illusions with no connection at all to the physical world
options.text: As illusions with no connection at all to the physical world
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Galileo didn't dismiss them entirely. He treated them as indirectly mathematizable, through changes in shape and motion.

options.html: As exact geometric shapes, like perfect circles and lines
options.text: As exact geometric shapes, like perfect circles and lines
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Shapes were idealized into geometry directly. Qualities were treated as indirectly mathematizable, through changes in shape and motion.

forms.stemHtml: Which claim is an example of what Husserl calls the surreptitious substitution?

options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. This claim uses the idealization without taking it for reality. The substitution has the form "X is really just Y," as in "color is really just wavelength."
Correct! The claim takes the idealized construct, wavelength, for the reality of color, forgetting that the concept was built by starting from seen color.

options.html: "Colors look different in daylight and lamplight."
options.text: "Colors look different in daylight and lamplight."
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. This describes lived experience. The substitution has the form "X is really just Y," as in "color is really just wavelength."
Sorry, that's incorrect. This describes scientific method. The substitution has the form "X is really just Y," as in "color is really just wavelength."

forms.stemHtml: What is the three-word English term (Carr's translation) for Husserl's image of the covering of mathematical idealizations that science lays over the world of experience?

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Husserl's Ideenkleid, the garb of ideas, fits the lifeworld so closely that it's taken for the world itself.
Correct! Husserl's Ideenkleid, the garb of ideas, fits the lifeworld so closely that it's taken for the world itself.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Husserl's image is the garb of ideas (Ideenkleid).

forms.stemHtml: In Husserl's account of pairing, how is another body apprehended as a lived body?

options.html: By reasoning that bodies like mine probably have minds
options.text: By reasoning that bodies like mine probably have minds
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Pairing isn't an inference. It's a passive, associative linking in which another body, similar to one's own lived body, is apprehended as lived.

options.html: By passive association with one's own lived body
options.text: By passive association with one's own lived body
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Pairing happens before any reasoning. Another body similar to one's own is immediately apprehended as lived.

options.html: By directly experiencing the other's feelings as one's own
options.text: By directly experiencing the other's feelings as one's own
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The other's experiences are never given as one's own. They're appresented. Pairing is a passive association with one's own lived body.

options.html: By observing the other's brain activity during behavior
options.text: By observing the other's brain activity during behavior
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Pairing is a feature of experience, not of observation. It's a passive association with one's own lived body.

title: Lifeworld and Others
